item.description:

This page is in flux; do not copy edit yet. The content is copied from the corresponding coffee page.

Bushland and grassland with scattered shrubs can be challenging to differentiate from coffee or cocoa systems, particularly in imagery with resolutions above 1 meter, where individual trees are not clearly visible. However, a key distinguishing feature is the lack of structured canopy organization typically associated with cultivated systems like coffee and cocoa. In high-resolution imagery, the natural, irregular arrangement of bushes and shrubs in bushland and grassland becomes apparent, contrasting with the clear planting patterns seen in agricultural systems.

item.title: Cocoa Tree Characteristics
item.description:
Commodity Recognition Book /cocoa_book/02_cocoa_cultivation/05_cocoa_appearance/ -

Cocoa trees are medium-sized, with mature heights typically ranging from four to eight meters, though some trees may grow as tall as twelve meters in favorable conditions. The tree has large, leathery leaves that are arranged alternately in a flat, two-row (distichous) pattern along the branches. The leaves are oval to elliptical in shape, measuring between 12 and 60 cm in length and between 4 and 20 cm in width. Leaf tips are pointed, and the bases are usually rounded or heart-shaped.

One of the most distinctive visual features is the color of young leaves, or flushes, which emerge reddish-pink before gradually turning light green as they mature.

item.title: Pruning Practices
item.description:
Commodity Recognition Book /coffee_book/02_coffee_cultivation/05_pruning/ -

Overview

Pruning is a common practice in coffee cultivation, typically performed annually after the harvest to maintain tree structure and optimize productivity, though its intensity and frequency vary across regions. In Colombia, for example, coffee trees are pruned frequently and kept short, maintaining a bush-like shape at around 1.5 meters in height. Conversely, in Vietnam, coffee trees are less frequently pruned and can grow taller, often exceeding two meters. These differences are evident in high-resolution imagery: heavily pruned coffee plantations display a more defined row pattern with visible soil between trees, whereas less frequently pruned systems exhibit a denser canopy, with larger, rounder, and “fluffier” tree crowns.

item.description:
Commodity Recognition Book /cocoa_book/01_cocoa_gallery/02_confounding_samples/06_seasonal/ -

This page is in flux; do not copy edit yet. The content is copied from the corresponding coffee page.

Seasonal agriculture can sometimes include crops with tall plants, such as cassava and sugarcane, which may resemble coffee systems due to their height and structure. However, seasonal agriculture typically exhibits a more uniform canopy compared to the often heterogeneous canopy of coffee. The defining characteristic of seasonal agriculture is its strong phenology, marked by rapid growth and harvesting cycles, usually completed within a year.

Fallow lands are often covered with secondary vegetation composed of small bushes, which can sometimes be misinterpreted as cocoa or coffee plantations. However, unlike tree crops, fallow lands typically lack a clear and organized canopy structure. Another key indicator for identifying fallow lands is their alternation with seasonal agriculture in a recurring cycle.

item.title: Irrigation Practices
item.description:
Commodity Recognition Book /coffee_book/02_coffee_cultivation/07_irrigation/ -

Overview

In highly intensified coffee systems, such as those in Vietnam, irrigation is often employed to sustain consistent productivity. When an irrigation system is in place, the coffee plot develops a more homogeneous phenology, behaving as a synchronized unit. Flowering, for instance, can be precisely triggered through irrigation management, resulting in the entire plot flowering simultaneously, even when neighboring plots have not yet begun. This synchronized flowering can be observed in high-resolution imagery, where the crop appears white due to the large amount of flowers.

item.title: Seasonal Cycles
item.description:
Commodity Recognition Book /coffee_book/02_coffee_cultivation/08_coffee_phenology/ -

Coffee phenology

Robusta coffee goes through a growth cycle of two years that can impact how it looks in satellite imagery. Understanding this cycle, called phenology, can help you interpret changes in canopy color, texture, and structure throughout the year.

For example, in Vietnam, where Robusta is the predominant coffee variety, the calendar can be divided into four main stages:

  • Flower-bud initiation (November–December): The new season begins as coffee plants prepare to flower. Buds start to form and develop.

  • Flowering (January–March): White flowers appear, often after the first rains. This period is short but important: it signals the start of the productive phase.

  • Fruit setting and development (April–August): The flowers turn into small green berries, which grow in size over the months. The canopy stays dense and green.

  • Ripening and harvest (September–November): Berries ripen, changing color from green to red or yellow, depending on the variety. This is when harvesting takes place.

The following figure shows a time-series of the average greenness of over four hundred Robusta coffee plots in Vietnam’s Central Highlands, based on NDVI (a common vegetation index). The seasonal NDVI pattern reflects key stages of the coffee growth cycle, from flowering to harvest.
